notes.meaning: The psalm opens with a simple cry of love: "I love the LORD." The reason is clear. God heard the psalmist when he begged for mercy in a hard time. Answered prayer draws our hearts to God. Loving God for what He has done is not selfish, because that is how creatures come to love their Maker.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note the late style of the Hebrew. They think the psalm was written after the exile, perhaps as thanks for Israel's return from Babylon, rather than by David.

notes.meaning: God "inclined His ear," like a kind friend leaning over a sick person to catch a faint whisper. Because God listened so closely, the psalmist promises to keep praying to Him for the rest of his life. Answered prayer is a reason to pray more, not less. He also chooses to call on this God alone.

The psalmist describes how close he came to dying. Death is pictured like ropes tying him up. "Sheol" means the grave, the place of the dead, and its pain seemed to grab hold of him. We do not know if the cause was sickness, enemies, or betrayal. The words show a trouble he could not escape on his own.

When things were at their worst, he turned to God in prayer. His prayer was short, humble and earnest: "O LORD, deliver my soul!" Real trouble often brings out real prayer. Prayer was not his last resort. It was the help he had always trusted.

Looking back on God's answer, the psalmist praises God's character. God is gracious, which means kind beyond what we deserve. He is righteous, meaning fair and true to His promises. He is full of compassion. The rescue came from God's goodness, not from the psalmist's own merit. He says "our God" because this mercy is for all God's people.

"The simplehearted" are honest, humble people who do not use tricks to save themselves. They trust God instead, even if the world thinks them foolish. God watches over such people. The psalmist counts himself among them: he was helpless, and God saved him.

The psalmist talks to his own soul and tells it to settle down again. His heart had been shaken by fear, but God has been good to him. True rest is found in God alone, not in the world. Matthew Henry says this is a fitting word to fall asleep with at night, and even at death.

He lists three things God rescued him from. His life was saved from death. His eyes were saved from tears, as his sorrow turned to joy. His feet were kept from stumbling, which may mean falling into the grave or falling into sin. One rescue turned out to hold many blessings.

Now that he is alive, he promises to "walk before the LORD." That means living each day knowing God sees him, and living to please God rather than people. "The land of the living" means this life on earth. A life God has spared should be lived for Him.

Even while he was suffering badly, the psalmist kept trusting God. His faith is what moved him to speak, both in prayer and in telling others. His faith was tested but not destroyed. Paul quotes this line in 2 Corinthians 4:13 about his own preaching.

In his panic he said, "All men are liars!" Many readers see this as a hasty word he later knew was too harsh. Even good people speak rashly in deep trouble. There is also some truth in it: anyone will let us down if we trust them in place of God. So his hope was in God alone.

Instead of asking why trouble came, he asks how he can thank God for so much good. He knows he can never pay God back or earn His favor. Still, a grateful heart wants to give God something that pleases Him.

His first answer is surprising: he will take something more from God. The "cup of salvation" was likely a cup lifted up and shared at a thanksgiving meal, or a drink offering poured out at the temple. It was a way to thank God for being rescued. The best way to "repay" God is to receive His gifts and keep calling on Him. Some Christians see a picture here of the cup at the Lord's Supper.

In his trouble he had made promises to God, called vows. Now he will keep them, right away and in public. He does this not to show off, but to show he is not ashamed of God and to invite others to praise too. A promise made to God is a debt to be paid.

"Saints" here means God's faithful people. "Precious" means very valuable. God does not lightly let His people die, and He watches over the time and way of their death. When they do die, He cares for them and receives them to Himself. Christians have long sung this verse at funerals and applied it to martyrs.

The psalmist gladly calls himself God's servant, and says it twice. He belongs to God in two ways. He was "born in the house," since his mother served God. And God set him free from his chains, the ropes of death. That freedom ties him to God even more closely, like a freed servant who chooses to stay with a good master for life.

He will bring a thank offering to God and keep calling on His name. In Israel this was a real sacrifice at the temple. For believers today, it means giving ourselves to God, praising Him, and doing good to others.

He repeats his promise to keep his vows in front of God's people. Now he names the place: the temple courts in Jerusalem. He was rescued in private, but his thanks will be public. The psalm ends with "Hallelujah," which means "Praise the LORD," and invites everyone to join in.
